opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think the best way to see it is to look at how fast the goalposts have been moving. Not that long ago, the question was whether these models could reliably do grade-school arithmetic word problems. They'd make silly mistakes adding two numbers. Then it became: can they do high school competition math? Then, can they do olympiad-level problems? And now the conversation is really about whether they can contribute to research-level mathematics, actual open questions that professional mathematicians care about.

So in the span of just a few years, we've gone from "this thing can't add" to "this thing can sometimes help me prove a lemma I was stuck on." That trajectory is, honestly, stunning. I've been doing math for my whole career, and I didn't expect to see it this fast.

That said, I want to be careful about how I frame it. Solving a competition problem is a very particular skill. The problem is well-posed, you know there's a solution, and it fits on a page. Research is different. You don't know whether the statement is even true, you have to decide which questions are worth asking, and sometimes you work for months on something that goes nowhere. So the real frontier now isn't "can it solve hard problems," it's "can it do the long, messy, exploratory work that research actually is."

And what I find most exciting is that we're starting to see glimpses of that. You give the model a genuine open problem, and occasionally it comes back with an idea, or a proof of a special case, or a connection to some other area that you hadn't considered. It's not replacing mathematicians, but it's becoming a real collaborator. For me, that's the right perspective: we've moved from AI as a calculator, to AI as a strong student, and now toward AI as a research partner. And I think the next few years are going to be about how far that last step goes.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the goalposts have moved from basic arithmetic and competition problems toward research mathematics, conveying that earlier benchmarks have become less remarkable.

r002.rationale: It describes early signs of models contributing ideas, proving special cases of open problems, and making unexpected connections, which communicates signs of inventing mathematics.

fable-5.1.text:
You know, I think the best way to put it in perspective is to just remember where we were a few years ago. In 2022, if you asked a model to add two three-digit numbers, it would often get it wrong. We were debating whether these systems could do arithmetic at all. And then GSM8K, grade school math word problems, became the benchmark everyone was chasing. That was considered hard.

Then we moved to competition math, the MATH dataset, AIME problems, and at each step people said, okay, this is the real test, this is where it will break. And every time, within a year or two, the benchmark was saturated. Now we're at the point where models are getting gold medal level performance at the International Mathematical Olympiad, and more importantly, they're starting to help with actual research questions. I've had the experience myself of giving a model an open problem from my own work, something I'd been stuck on, and getting back a proof that was correct and that I hadn't seen.

So the way I think about it is that there's a ladder. Arithmetic, then word problems, then competition math, then research level problems. And what's striking is not any single rung, it's the speed at which we've climbed. Each rung used to be a separate research program with its own decade of effort, and now it's a matter of months between them.

The honest caveat is that the models are still uneven. They can solve something that would take a PhD student a week and then make a silly mistake on something simpler. So you have to be careful about what "mathematical ability" means. But the trajectory is really the point. If you had told me in 2022 that by now we'd be seriously discussing whether AI could contribute to the frontier of mathematics, I would have said that's decades away. And it's happening.

r001.rationale: The response says that problems once treated as hard benchmarks are now saturated within a year or two, illustrating that earlier impressive abilities have become routine.

r002.rationale: It says models are beginning to help with research questions and describes one producing a correct proof for an open problem that the speaker had not seen, showing signs of novel mathematical contribution.

astra-6.text:
I think the striking thing is how quickly the question has changed. A few years ago, we were asking whether these models could reliably solve fairly elementary math problems. Now we’re asking how far they can go on problems that require real ingenuity: choosing the right representation, finding an intermediate result, or abandoning an approach that isn’t working.

But mathematical ability is not one single thing. Solving a problem with a known answer is different from producing a rigorous proof, and both are different from doing research, where you have to decide what questions are worth asking in the first place. So I would be careful about turning success on a particular test into a claim that mathematics is solved.

For me, the exciting part is the possibility of a model becoming a mathematical collaborator—something you can explore an idea with, that can challenge your intuition or suggest a connection you hadn’t considered. That’s a much richer notion of progress than just getting more answers right.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts earlier questions about elementary problems with current questions about ingenuity, but does not say those earlier abilities are now taken for granted.

r002.rationale: It describes possible collaboration and suggesting connections, but does not state that models are beginning to show signs of inventing new mathematics.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the striking thing is how quickly we’ve gone from models that struggled with fairly basic mathematical reasoning to models that can work through difficult, multistep problems. But there are different levels of mathematical ability. Solving a problem when someone has already posed a precise question is one thing. Finding the right question, inventing a useful definition, or recognizing that an unexpected connection matters—that’s another.

So I would put the progress in perspective along those two axes: how hard are the problems the models can solve, and how independently can they do meaningful mathematics? Progress on the first has been remarkable. The second is a much deeper challenge, because mathematics is not just producing a correct answer. It’s also deciding what is worth understanding.

r001.rationale: It describes rapid progress from basic reasoning to difficult multistep problems, but does not say that abilities once considered impressive are now taken for granted.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes solving posed problems from inventing definitions or finding questions, but does not say models are beginning to show signs of inventing new mathematics.
